newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S., Japan move towards new aviation deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan move towards new aviation deal.

text.p: After two decades of bickering, Japan and the United States appear to be finally moving closer to a pact aimed at bringing widespread deregulation in aviation, analysts say.
Last month the two sides agreed to strike an interim deal covering both passenger and cargo traffic by the end of September, with formal talks set for August 4 to 6 in Tokyo.
"This time it seems they have really come a step forward," said Mami Yoda, associate director of corporate ratings at Standard & Poor's.
The "agreement to agree" boosted hopes in Japan that Washington may accept a more limited deal than "open skies" -- its much trumpeted free-market goal.

It has struck open skies deals with a number of European nations and has begun wooing smaller Asian countries, but Japan has refused, saying it supports deregulation but believes that lifting all government restrictions would only lead to alliances dominated by U.S. carriers.

Smarting from what many agree to be an unfair bilateral treaty signed during the U.S. occupation period, Japan has pushed for equality for its carriers, demanding more rights for All Nippon Airways (ANA).
The treaty gives two U.S. airlines, UAL Corp's United Airlines and Northwest Airlines wide rights, with only Japan Airlines (JAL) getting similar treatment.

It also gives wide rights to U.S. cargo carrier Federal Express (Fedex), while U.S carriers, AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines, along with ANA, have limited rights.
In addition to the lucrative routes between the two nations, access to the Asia-Pacific market is also at stake.

The International Air Transport Association (IATA) predicts traffic between Japan and the United States will double by 2010, and that the Asia-Pacific region will account for 50 percent of the world's passenger traffic by the same year.
Because of that, analysts said most U.S. airlines have stepped up pressure to accept an interim deal, arguing it was better to get something now than possibly nothing later.
Only Northwest, which now has the most U.S.-Japan flights, insists on settling for nothing less than open skies.

The analysts said an interim deal was more likely because U.S. officials are trying to help cargo carrier Fedex. The Japanese side says Washington has made more Fedex routes, particularly to China, a priority in the talks.

Fedex has aggressive expansion plans for the region. "In particular, China, Japan and the Philippines and the many Asian economies that are out outpacing the other economies in the world," said spokesman David Clarke.
Analysts said the bare bones of an interim deal, based on a Japanese proposal, have begun to emerge.
According to a Japanese transport ministry official, the proposal would allow unlimited access between the two nations for four carriers: JAL, ANA, United and Northwest.
He also said that depending on U.S. flexibility over open skies, there was room for more routes and frequencies for American, Continental and Delta.
This would also extend to Fedex, with more routes beyond Japan to other countries possible, he said.
"Japan is willing to be flexible on Fedex and other carriers that have lesser rights under the treaty but it is a prerequisite that the United States also is flexible." he said.

On the question of the much-desired flights beyond Japan to other Asian cities, he said Tokyo was willing to offer more routes for United and Northwest -- enough to be commercially viable -- although the number would be capped.

But the official added a final deal would not be reached quickly. "It's good the talks have reached a formal level and that we've set the September goal but there are still large gaps on matters of substance," he said.
